summary.text: Lesson 2-7 of enVision Math Grade 4: subtracting when the top number is full of zeros — the borrow ripple that turns middle zeros into 9s, the slide-both-down-1 shortcut, and counting up when the numbers are close.

why.text: Across-zero subtraction is where the algorithm feels hardest — and where the best move is often not the algorithm at all. Knowing three routes and choosing between them is the difference between doing math and following it.

objectives.text: Subtract across zeros by regrouping, with middle zeros becoming 9s
Use the slide trick: subtract 1 from both numbers to avoid borrowing
Choose counting up when the numbers are close
Explain why sliding both numbers preserves a difference

parentNote.text: Built from the Topic 2 textbook scan, Lesson 2-7 — the last lesson of the topic. The slide trick (6,000 − 4,678 = 5,999 − 4,677) is the star; the WHY behind it was planted in 2-5's gap picture, so ask her to explain it rather than just use it. The error question has a fingerprint worth naming out loud: an answer too big by double one piece means that piece traveled the wrong way.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz in one sitting. Try the slide trick on paper once — feel the borrows vanish.

cards.def:
**A zero has nothing to lend — the borrow travels left until it finds a digit that does.**
• To take anything from 6,000, the trade starts at the 6 and ripples right.
• After the ripple: 5 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones. Same value, ready to subtract.

**Subtracting 1 from BOTH numbers keeps the difference and deletes the zeros problem.**
• 6,000 − 4,678 = 5,999 − 4,677 — and 5,999 never needs a single borrow.
• The gap between the numbers did not move, because both ends slid together.
cards.hint: One tiny slide, zero regroups. This trick alone is worth the lesson.

cards.def:
**When the numbers are close, count up and skip the borrowing entirely.**
• 3,000 − 1,998: from 1,998, hop 2 to reach 2,000, then 1,000 more — 1,002.
• The worst across-zero subtractions are often the easiest count-ups.

**A difference is a gap, and a gap does not care where it sits on the number line.**
• Slide both numbers down 1, down 3, up 10 — the gap is identical every time.
• This is lesson 2-5's number-line picture, turned into a technique.

questions.q: A school fundraiser aims to raise $6,000 and has $4,678 so far. How much is left to raise?
questions.hint: Either regroup across the zeros, or slide both numbers down 1.
steps: The slide: 6,000 − 4,678 has the same answer as 5,999 − 4,677.
5,999 − 4,677 needs no borrowing at all: 1,322.
The regroup route lands in the same place: 1,322.

ex.main: **$1,322.** The slide turned a triple-borrow monster into a no-borrow stroll.
ex.tip: Whenever the top number is all zeros after its first digit, think slide first, algorithm second.

questions.hint: The zeros will pass the borrow along — or slide both down 1.
steps: Slide: 499 − 235 has the same gap.
Ones: 9 − 5 = 4. Tens: 9 − 3 = 6. Hundreds: 4 − 2 = 2.
Difference: 264.

ex.main: **264.** No borrows after the slide — the zeros never got a vote.
ex.tip: Check: 264 + 236 = 500. Nice round checks are the fastest kind.

questions.q: To subtract anything from 6,000 by regrouping, what does the top number become?
questions.hint: Follow the borrow as it ripples right from the 6.
steps: The ones need 10, but the tens have nothing — nor do the hundreds.
The 6 thousands lend one: 5 thousands, 10 hundreds.
A hundred lends: 9 hundreds, 10 tens. A ten lends: 9 tens, 10 ones.
Result: 5 | 9 | 9 | 10 — still exactly 6,000, dressed for subtraction.

ex.main: **5 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones.** Every middle zero becomes a 9; the last place gets the 10.
ex.tip: The 9s are the signature of borrowing across zeros. If your regrouped middle digits are not 9s, retrace the ripple.

questions.q: Why does 6,000 − 4,678 give the same answer as 5,999 − 4,677?
opts: Both numbers slid down by 1, so the gap between them did not move
It does not — the answers differ by 1
Because subtraction ignores the ones place
questions.hint: Picture the two numbers on a number line, both stepping left once.
steps: A difference measures the gap between two points on the number line.
Move both points down 1: each end of the gap shifts equally.
The gap itself — the answer — is untouched: 1,322 both ways.
The payoff: 5,999 has no zeros, so nothing needs to borrow.

ex.main: **Both slid together, so the gap held still.** The trick is the number-line picture wearing work clothes.
ex.tip: Slide by whatever amount kills the zeros — down 1 is almost always the right dose.

questions.hint: Slide both down 1 and the zeros vanish.
steps: 7,999 − 3,546 has the same gap.
Ones: 9 − 6 = 3. Tens: 9 − 4 = 5. Hundreds: 9 − 5 = 4. Thousands: 7 − 3 = 4.
Difference: 4,453.

ex.main: **4,453.** Four clean columns instead of a borrow chain.
ex.tip: Check: 4,453 + 3,547 = 8,000. When the check is this tidy, enjoy it.

questions.q: A warehouse holds 40,500 boxes and ships 26,384. How many remain?
questions.hint: Only some columns touch a zero — scout first.
steps: Ones: 0 − 4 needs a borrow, and the tens are 0 too — the ripple runs left to the 5 hundreds.
After the ripple: 4 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones. Ones: 10 − 4 = 6. Tens: 9 − 8 = 1. Hundreds: 4 − 3 = 1.
Thousands: 0 − 6 borrows from the 4 ten thousands: 10 − 6 = 4. Ten thousands: 3 − 2 = 1.

ex.main: **14,116.** Two separate borrow ripples — one through the trailing zeros, one at the thousands.
ex.tip: Zeros in the middle of a number each get their own ripple. Scout them before starting and none of them surprises you.

questions.hint: The two middle zeros will both turn into 9s.
steps: Ones: 3 − 5 — the borrow ripples through the two zeros to the 7.
The top becomes 6 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones.
Ones: 13 − 5 = 8. Tens: 9 − 7 = 2. Hundreds: 9 − 6 = 3. Thousands: 6 − 2 = 4.
Difference: 4,328.

ex.main: **4,328.** The middle zeros became 9s — the across-zeros signature, right on schedule.
ex.tip: Or slide both down 4: 6,999 − 2,671 = 4,328. Any slide that empties the zeros is legal.

questions.q: For 5,000 − 2,368, Amara answers 3,368. What did she actually compute?
opts: 5,000 − 2,000 + 368 — she subtracted the thousands but ADDED the rest back instead of subtracting it
questions.hint: Compare her answer to the true one and measure the miss.
steps: The true difference: 5,000 − 2,368 = 2,632.
Amara's 3,368 is too big by 736 — which is exactly 2 × 368.
That fingerprint means the 368 went the wrong way: subtracted the 2,000, then added 368 back.
All of 2,368 must leave: the thousands AND the 368. Check: 2,632 + 2,368 = 5,000.

ex.main: **She added the 368 back instead of subtracting it — the truth is 2,632.** Splitting a number is fine; both pieces must still leave.
ex.tip: An error of exactly double one piece of the number means that piece traveled the wrong direction. Fingerprints like this make errors readable.

questions.q: Which strategy makes 3,000 − 1,998 the easiest, and what is the answer?
opts: Count up: 2 to reach 2,000, then 1,000 more — 1,002
questions.hint: The numbers are close together. What does that suggest?
steps: 1,998 sits only 2 below 2,000, and 2,000 is 1,000 below 3,000.
Count up: 2 + 1,000 = 1,002. Two hops, no borrowing.
Regrouping also reaches 1,002, but through a triple borrow chain — legal, just slow.
Rounding to "1,000" throws away the 2 — an estimate posing as an answer.

ex.main: **Counting up: 1,002.** When numbers are close, the gap is small enough to walk.
ex.tip: The slide-up-by-2 option computes 3,002 − 2,000 correctly as 1,002 — but the option SAYS 998, and a right method quoted with a wrong result is still wrong.

questions.q: Which subtraction has EXACTLY the same answer as 70,000 − 23,456?
questions.hint: Only a slide that moves BOTH numbers the same amount keeps the gap.
steps: 70,000 − 23,456 = 46,544 — that is the gap to preserve.
69,999 − 23,455 slides both down 1: gap intact, 46,544.
69,999 − 23,456 slides only the top: gap shrinks to 46,543.
70,001 − 23,455 slides the ends apart: gap grows to 46,546. And 69,000 − 23,000 is a rounded estimate, not an equal.

ex.main: **69,999 − 23,455.** Same slide on both ends, same gap — everything else moved one end and lost the equality.
ex.tip: The test for any rewrite: did both numbers move by the same amount in the same direction? If not, the answer moved too.
